Decayed turns a cumulative counter, read at irregular times, into an
exponentially decayed average rate.
Many system statistics are published as running totals rather than rates:
microseconds spent stalled on memory or I/O since boot, bytes sent, requests
served. What a reader wants is "the share of time stalled over the last
minute" or "requests per second lately", which is what operating systems
report alongside such totals as 10, 60 and 300 second averages. Decayed
computes that from the totals alone. For a counter of microseconds stalled,
the rate is microseconds per second, so dividing by 1e6 gives the share of
time (multiply by 100 for a percentage).
Each Update takes the rate over the interval since the last one,
r = Δtotal/Δt, and blends it into the average with
e = exp(−Δt/window),   a = a·e + r·(1−e).
This is exact for irregular sampling: it is the continuous-time exponential
average with time constant window of a rate that was r throughout the
interval, which is all a pair of counter readings can say about it. A fixed
per-sample weight, as in EWMA, would be wrong under jitter: a reading
delayed to 3 s would count the same as one taken after 1 s, and a burst of
readings close together would drag the average towards whatever those
moments happened to show. Here a reading's weight is the time it covers.
After one window of a new constant rate the average has moved 1 − 1/e, about
63%, of the way from the old rate to the new one, whatever the spacing of the
readings; after three windows, 95%. The first rate initialises the average
directly rather than being blended into an implicit zero, which would read
as a quiet system for the first window and then as a rise that never
happened.
A total lower than the previous one means the counter was reset, or wrapped
past its maximum. With one reading the two cannot be told apart, so both are
treated as a reset: the reading becomes a new baseline, no rate is produced,
and Resets is incremented. A counter that wraps loses one interval, never
yields an absurd rate.
Time comes only from the at argument; nothing here reads the clock, so it
is as testable as the caller's clock is. Intervals are taken with
time.Time.Sub, which uses the monotonic reading that time.Now attaches, so a
wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort the interval.
Readings at or before the previous one (a clock stepped backwards, a
duplicate) are skipped and counted in Skipped, and leave the baseline where
it was: the next valid reading covers their interval.
Method: the exponential smoothing of irregularly spaced data of D. J. Wright,
"Forecasting data published at irregular time intervals using an extension
of Holt's method", Management Science 32(4), 1986, here applied to the
interval-average rate, which makes the step response exact rather than
approximate.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewDecayed. Safe to copy, not
safe for concurrent use.
Defined in drift/decayed.go.
EWMA
type EWMA struct

EWMA is an exponentially weighted moving average: each new value moves the
average a fixed fraction alpha of the way towards itself,
vt = v{t−1} + alpha·(xt − v{t−1}),
so a value k samples old carries weight alpha·(1−alpha)^k. It describes a
level; it does not test one. For a decision about whether the level moved,
use EWMAChart, which adds the control limits this lacks.
The first value initialises the average rather than being blended with an
implicit zero, so a series that starts at 500 does not spend its first few
dozen samples climbing up from nothing. The average counts samples, not
time: for readings at irregular times, Decayed is the right tool.
Method: the exponentially weighted average as used in forecasting by R. G.
Brown, Statistical Forecasting for Inventory Control, McGraw-Hill, 1959.
The zero value is not usable (its alpha is 0); build one with NewEWMA or
NewEWMAHalfLife. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are
skipped and counted in Skipped.
Defined in drift/ewma.go.
EWMAChart
type EWMAChart struct

EWMAChart is an exponentially weighted moving average control chart: it
signals when a smoothed series leaves a band around a target level.
The statistic is
zt = λ·x_t + (1−λ)·z{t−1},   z_0 = target,
and the band at sample t is
target ± L·σ·sqrt( λ/(2−λ) · (1 − (1−λ)^(2t)) ).
σ times the square root is the exact standard deviation of z_t when the x_t
are independent with standard deviation σ. It starts at λσ and widens towards
the asymptotic σ·sqrt(λ/(2−λ)); using the asymptotic band from the first
sample would leave the chart nearly blind to a shift present from the start.
Use it for small shifts that persist. Averaging over about 2/λ samples lets
it see a shift of half a standard deviation that a chart of raw values
would never flag, at the price of reacting more slowly than a raw-value
check to a single large spike. For a shift of one known size CUSUM is the
faster detector; the two have similar performance across a range of sizes.
Method: S. W. Roberts, "Control chart tests based on geometric moving
averages", Technometrics 1(3), 1959. Exact-variance limits and run-length
tables: J. M. Lucas and M. S. Saccucci, "Exponentially weighted moving
average control schemes: properties and enhancements", Technometrics 32(1),

Presentation follows D. C. Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical
Quality Control, Wiley, chapter on CUSUM and EWMA charts.

target and σ are the in-control mean and standard deviation of the series,
and they are yours to supply: estimate them from a stretch you know to be
normal (Welford does that), not from the stretch under test. The chart
assumes independent samples; a strongly autocorrelated series inflates the
spread of z_t beyond what the limits allow for and signals too often.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewEWMAChart or
DefaultEWMAChart. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf
are skipped and counted in Skipped, and do not advance t. Finite inputs
within a factor of a few of the float64 limit can overflow z_t; rescale
such a series first.
Defined in drift/chart.go.
PageHinkley
type PageHinkley struct

PageHinkley is the Page–Hinkley test for a change in the mean of a series
whose level is not known in advance.
It is CUSUM with the target replaced by the running mean of everything seen
since the last Reset. With mean_t the mean of x_1..x_t, it keeps
m⁺_t = Σ (x_i − mean_i − δ),   M⁺_t = min(0, m⁺_1, …, m⁺_t)
m⁻_t = Σ (x_i − mean_i + δ),   M⁻_t = max(0, m⁻_1, …, m⁻_t)
and signals Up when m⁺_t − M⁺_t > λ and Down when M⁻_t − m⁻_t > λ (the
larger when both, Up on a tie). δ plays the part of CUSUM's k, the size of
deviation tolerated without accumulating evidence, and λ the part of h.
Use it when there is no target to supply: a series per process, per disk,
per tenant, each settling at its own level. The price is that the reference
level is learned from the series itself. Shortly after Reset it rests on a
handful of samples, so the test is noisier than CUSUM with a true target.
After a change the running mean slowly absorbs the new level, the evidence
stops growing and then drains, and the next change would be measured
against a blend of both regimes. Reset after acting on a signal. When the
target is known, CUSUM is the sharper test.
Method: E. S. Page, "Continuous inspection schemes", Biometrika 41(1/2),
1954; D. V. Hinkley, "Inference about the change-point from cumulative sum
tests", Biometrika 58(3), 1971. The running-mean formulation is the one
given by J. Gama, I. Žliobaitė, A. Bifet, M. Pechenizkiy and A. Bouchachia,
"A survey on concept drift adaptation", ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), 2014.
δ and λ are in the data's units and the caller's to choose. There is no
literature default worth the name, since both scale with the noise. δ =
σ/2 and λ = 5σ, the CUSUM defaults, are a reasonable start: at those values
the in-control average run length measured here is about 480 samples, close
to CUSUM's 465, and a one-sigma shift after 100 in-control samples is
detected in about 11 to 12 (TestPageHinkleyARL). The delay grows when the
shift comes early, while the mean still rests on few samples.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewPageHinkley. Safe to copy,
not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in
Skipped. Finite inputs within a factor of a few of the float64 limit can
overflow the sums; rescale such a series first.
Defined in drift/pagehinkley.go.
Signal
type Signal int

Signal is what a detector says about the sample it was just given.
It is a statistic crossing a threshold the caller chose, not a probability
and not a verdict: Up means "the evidence for an upward shift is now larger
than you said it had to be", and what to do about that is the caller's.

Welford
type Welford struct

Welford is a running mean and variance in one pass and fixed memory.
The obvious one-pass method keeps Σx and Σx² and takes
(Σx² − (Σx)²/n)/(n−1) at the end. On data far from zero that subtracts two
nearly equal huge numbers, and the variance it returns is mostly rounding:
readings that move by a few units around 1e9 lose every significant digit
of their spread, and the result can even come out negative. Welford's
update keeps the mean and the sum of squared deviations from it instead,
so nothing large is ever subtracted from anything large.
Method: B. P. Welford, "Note on a method for calculating corrected sums of
squares and products", Technometrics 4(3), 1962. Merge is the pairwise
combination of T. F. Chan, G. H. Golub and R. J. LeVeque, "Updating
formulae and a pairwise algorithm for computing sample variances", Stanford
report STAN-CS-79-773, 1979, published as "Algorithms for computing the
sample variance: analysis and recommendations", The American Statistician
37(3), 1983.
The zero value is an empty accumulator, ready to use. A Welford is a plain
value and safe to copy, which is how a snapshot is taken; it is not safe
for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped, never
folded in: one NaN would otherwise poison the mean for the rest of the
series. Finite values whose squared spread overflows float64 (beyond about
1e154) give a variance of +Inf, never NaN or a negative number; the mean
stays finite. Rescale such data first if the variance matters.

runi/rate
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/rate"

Package rate turns cumulative counters into per-interval rates, and keeps
bounded-memory summaries of those rates.
Many system statistics are published as running totals rather than rates:
bytes and packets sent, CPU time in nanoseconds, time stalled in
microseconds, context switches. A poller reads each total on every tick and
wants the rate over the tick, together with a short memory of what the rate
has been: the highest and lowest of the last minute, the peak since the last
report, whether the poller itself is keeping time. Nothing here sleeps or
reads the clock: the caller passes each reading with the time it was taken,
so every type is as testable as the caller's clock is. Every update does
O(1) work (amortised, for Window) in fixed memory and allocates nothing.
Which to use:

Counter turns successive totals into a Reading: the increase, the
interval it covers, and the increase per second. It knows the counter's
width, so a 32-bit counter that wraps past its maximum still yields the
right increase, and it tells a wrap from a reset (the counter restarted
from zero) by how large the increase would have to be.
Window is the minimum and maximum of the last n values, exact, in
amortised O(1) per value: "the highest rate in the last 60 readings".
Peak is the maximum since you last called Reset, and when it happened:
"the peak since the last report".
Intervals watches the gaps between readings rather than the readings:
a producer that has stalled shows up as a long last interval, one that
is bursting as a short mean.

Rates here are raw: the rate over one interval, no smoothing. For a rate
that forgets gradually — the 10, 60 and 300 second averages operating
systems publish beside such totals — use Decayed from
github.com/org-runink/runi/drift, which takes the same totals directly.
Use Counter when you need each interval's own rate (to keep a peak or a
windowed maximum, to export it, to feed a detector), or when the counter is
narrower than 64 bits and wraps: Decayed treats every decrease as a reset.
c,  := rate.NewCounter(32)
w,  := rate.NewWindow(60)
for tick := range ticks {
    if r, ok := c.Update(readOctets(), tick); ok {
        w.Add(r.PerSecond)
    }
}
log.Printf("busiest second of the last minute: %.0f B/s", w.Max())
Every type that takes float64 values skips NaN and ±Inf rather than folding
them in, and counts them in Skipped: a missed reading should not poison a
summary, and a series that is mostly NaN should be visible as one. Readings
whose time is not after the previous reading are skipped and counted too.
Counter, Peak and Intervals are plain values, safe to copy; NewWindow
returns a *Window, which holds its buffer by reference and is shared, not
copied. None is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or
guard it.
What this package does not do
It cannot see more than two readings say. A counter read once per interval
that wraps twice in that interval, or wraps once by more than half its
range, or is reset and then climbs past its old value before the next
reading, gives a wrong increase or none, and nothing in the readings can
show it. Read a counter often enough that it cannot move by half its range
between two readings; Counter's doc gives the arithmetic.
It does not smooth, forecast or alert. A Reading is the rate over one
interval, as noisy as the interval is short; for smoothing see drift.Decayed
and drift.EWMA, and for "has this rate changed?" the detectors in drift.
Window counts readings, not time. "The last 60 values" is "the last minute"
only when readings arrive once a second; under irregular polling a time
window would need to hold a variable number of values, which this package
does not do in fixed memory.
It does not interpolate. A rate is attributed to the whole interval it was
measured over; a burst inside the interval is averaged over it, and a peak
shorter than the polling interval is never seen at its full height.
It does not read counters. Where the totals come from — files, sockets,
device registers — is the caller's business.

Counter
type Counter struct

Counter turns successive readings of a cumulative counter into
per-interval increases and rates, across wraps and resets.
A counter of width w bits counts modulo 2^w: after 2^w − 1 it wraps to 0
and carries on, as RFC 2578 §7.1.6 defines for SNMP's Counter32 ("when it
reaches a maximum value of 2^32-1 ... it wraps around and starts increasing
again from zero"). Many kernel and device counters behave the same way at
32 bits, and most modern ones at 64. When a reading is below the previous
one, the increase across one wrap is (2^w − previous) + total, which is
(total − previous) mod 2^w.
But a reading below the previous one is also what a reset looks like: the
device, process or kernel restarted and the counter began again from zero.
Two readings cannot tell a wrap from a reset to a small number, so Counter
uses a heuristic, and it is only that: a decrease is taken as a wrap when
the increase it implies is at most half the modulus, 2^(w−1), and as a
reset otherwise. Put the other way round, a fall of less than half the
range is a reset and a fall of half the range or more is a wrap. The
reasoning is the standard assumption that the counter is read often enough
to wrap at most once per interval: a reader that keeps to it comfortably
sees increases well below half the range, so a wrap implying more than
that is more likely a reset. The rule is wrong both ways at the margin. A
genuine wrap by more than half the range is taken as a reset, and that
interval is lost. A reset of a counter that stood in the top half of its
range is taken as a wrap when the new total is at least half the range
below the old one, and that interval's increase is overstated by up to
half the range. Read the counter often enough that it moves by well under
half its range between readings: a 32-bit octet counter on a 10 Gbit/s
link (1.25e9 bytes per second) wraps every 3.4 s and must be read at least
every 1.7 s, which is why RFC 2863 defines 64-bit "high capacity"
interface counters. Where a counter is known not to wrap in practice,
width 64 makes every decrease a reset.
A 64-bit counter is never taken to have wrapped: every decrease is a reset.
At 100 Gbit/s, 1.25e10 bytes per second, a 64-bit byte counter wraps once
in 2^64 / 1.25e10 ≈ 1.5e9 s, about 47 years; a 64-bit count of nanoseconds
of CPU time wraps once in 584 years of one CPU's time. No interval between
two readings is that long, and a decrease is a restart.
The first reading, and the first after a reset, is a baseline and yields
no rate. A reading whose time is not after the previous one (a duplicate,
a clock stepped backwards) is skipped and counted in Skipped, leaving the
baseline where it was: the next valid reading covers its interval. A total
above 2^w − 1 cannot come from a w-bit counter; it is skipped and counted
in Invalid, before any other check, and also leaves the baseline alone.
Intervals come from time.Time.Sub, which uses the monotonic reading that
time.Now attaches, so a wall-clock step between two such readings does
not distort them.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewCounter. Safe to copy, not
safe for concurrent use.
Defined in rate/counter.go.
Intervals
type Intervals struct

Intervals summarises the gaps between reading times: the last, the mean,
the shortest and the longest.
A rate is only as good as the readings behind it. A poller that should read
every second but is itself starved for CPU reads every five, and the rates
it reports are then five-second averages that hide every burst shorter than
that; a producer that has stalled sends nothing, and the next reading
covers the whole stall. Watching the gaps shows both: Late says the last
gap exceeded what you expect, Max shows the worst since Reset, and a Mean
well below the nominal period shows readings arriving in bursts.
The mean is exact: the sum of the gaps is held as a 128-bit integer count
of nanoseconds and divided by N only when Mean is called, truncating to the
nanosecond. Each gap is at most math.MaxInt64 ns, so 2^63 gaps of the
largest size still sum to under 2^126: the sum cannot overflow for any
input, and nothing is lost to rounding as a running float64 mean would.
The first time is a baseline. A time not after the previous one (a
duplicate, a clock stepped backwards, readings delivered out of order) is
skipped, counted in Skipped, and leaves the baseline where it was, so the
next valid time's gap covers it. Gaps come from time.Time.Sub, which uses
the monotonic reading that time.Now attaches, and like it saturate at about
292 years.
Late can only judge a gap that has closed. A producer that stops entirely
never calls Add, and Late keeps reporting the gap before it; to see a gap
that is still open, compare the current time with the time of your last
reading.
The zero value is empty and ready to use. Safe to copy, not safe for
concurrent use.
Defined in rate/intervals.go.
Peak
type Peak struct

Peak is the largest value seen since the last Reset, and the time it was
seen.
It is the summary a periodic report wants: "the busiest second since the
last report, and when", after which the report calls Reset. It does not
decay and does not forget on its own; for the largest of the last n values
use Window, and for a level that forgets gradually use drift.Decayed.
Ties keep the first: a value equal to the peak does not move At, so At is
the time given with the first value to reach the peak. Times are stored as
given and need not increase; a larger value replaces the peak whatever its
time. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped.
The zero value is an empty peak, ready to use. Safe to copy, not safe for
concurrent use.
Defined in rate/peak.go.
Reading
type Reading struct

Reading is what one pair of counter readings says: the counter rose by
Delta over Interval, which is PerSecond per second.
Defined in rate/counter.go.
Window
type Window struct

Window is the minimum and maximum of the last Size values added, exact,
in amortised O(1) time per value and fixed memory.
Rescanning the last n values on every Add costs O(n) per value; a sorted
structure costs O(log n). Window keeps instead two monotonic queues of
candidates. A value can only ever be the window's maximum if no later
value is at least as large, so when x arrives every queued maximum
candidate ≤ x is dropped from the back, and a candidate that has left the
window is dropped from the front. What remains is decreasing from front to
back, its front is the maximum, and each value enters and leaves each queue
once: amortised O(1), and at most Size candidates per queue. The minimum is
the mirror image.
Method: the monotonic wedge of D. Lemire, "Streaming maximum-minimum filter
using no more than three comparisons per element", Nordic Journal of
Computing 13(4), 2006. The block method of J. Gil and M. Werman, "Computing
2-D min, median, and max filters", IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis
and Machine Intelligence 15(5), 1993, reaches a similar constant cost per
value, but it processes values in blocks of the window size and so answers
late for a stream; the wedge answers after every value.
Ties: when x equals a queued candidate, the older one is dropped and x is
kept, because x stays in the window longer and the queue stays shorter.
Equal values are interchangeable, so which is kept never changes Min or
Max; +0 and −0 compare equal and either may be returned for the other.
The window counts accepted values: NaN and ±Inf are skipped, counted in
Skipped, and do not take a slot, so "the last 60 values" means the last 60
finite ones.
Both queues live in one buffer of 2·Size slots, 16 bytes each, allocated by
NewWindow; Add and Reset never allocate. NewWindow returns a pointer, and
a Window is used through it: a copy of the struct would share the buffer
with the original, and using both would corrupt both. Build one per series
with NewWindow.
The zero value is not usable (Add panics on it); build one with
NewWindow. Not safe to copy and not safe for concurrent use.
Defined in rate/window.go.

docs/api/tree/.body:
runi/tree
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/tree"

Package tree attributes a quantity measured per node of a hierarchy to the
subtrees that cause it, and keeps that attribution current as single nodes
change.
Many quantities are measured per node of a hierarchy but asked about per
subtree: resource use or pressure per group in a hierarchy of process
groups, bytes per directory, cost per team in an organisation. "How much
does this group use, all of it included?" is a subtree sum; "which part of
it is responsible?" is the largest values below it. Recomputing either from
scratch is O(n) per question. A Tree keeps every node's subtree sum and
subtree maximum up to date as values and structure change, at a cost of
the node's depth per change, so the questions become O(1) (sum, maximum)
or O(subtree) (top k), and every answer is deterministic: children are
kept in key order and every tie goes to the smaller key.
Which to use:

Tree holds the hierarchy (Add, AddRoot, Move, Remove, RemoveSubtree)
and the values (Set). Sum and Own are the subtree total and the node's
own share; Max is the single largest own value below a node and where
it is; TopK is the k heaviest descendants by own value or by subtree
sum; Path and Depth say where a node sits.
Snapshot copies the structure, without values, and Diff compares two
copies: which nodes appeared, disappeared, or moved to another parent.
It is how to report what changed in a hierarchy between two polls.

Bytes per directory, and the directories that hold most of them:
t := tree.New[string]()
t.AddRoot("/")
t.Add("/var", "/")
t.Add("/var/log", "/var")
t.Set("/var/log", 7e9)
fmt.Println(t.Sum("/")) // 7e+09
top := t.TopK("/", 3, tree.BySum, nil)

A Tree is a forest: it may have several roots. A root is its own parent
wherever a parent is named: Parent of a root returns the root, Add(id, id)
adds one, Move(id, id) makes one, and Diff reports a node that became a
root as moved to itself.
Sums are kept with compensated summation, so a million updates to large
values do not round away the small values beside them; Set gives the
bound, and a test holds it. Set rejects NaN and ±Inf with ErrInvalid
instead of skipping them as this module's streaming summaries do: a value
here is state shared by every ancestor's sum, and a NaN added once could
never be subtracted out again. Every error wraps ErrInvalid, and the
specific ones (ErrUnknown, ErrExists, ErrCycle, ErrHasChildren) can each
be matched with errors.Is.
Set, Sum, Own, Max, Parent and Depth do not allocate, and neither do
Children, Path and TopK when the destination slice has room; a test holds
each of these to zero. A Tree is not safe for concurrent use; guard it.
What this package does not do
It does not read hierarchies. Walking a filesystem, a process-group
hierarchy or an organisation chart, and deciding when, is the caller's
business; a Tree is told about each node and each value.
It keeps sums and maxima only. Both can be updated along one path to the
root; a median or a percentile of a subtree cannot, and needs a mergeable
quantile sketch per node, such as the KLL sketch (Karnin, Lang and
Liberty, 2016) or the t-digest (Dunning and Ertl, 2019), which this
package does not provide. A minimum is a maximum of negated values: keep a
second Tree. A mean is Sum divided by a count kept as a second Tree whose
every value is 1.
It is fast for bushy hierarchies, not for long chains. Every update costs
the depth of the node, which for directory trees and group hierarchies is
a handful; on a path of a hundred thousand nodes it is a hundred thousand.
Where depth is unbounded, link-cut trees (D. D. Sleator and R. E. Tarjan,
"A data structure for dynamic trees", J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 26(3), 1983)
or Euler-tour trees answer the same path and subtree aggregates in
O(log n) amortised per update, at a large constant and in far more code.
TopK walks the subtree it is asked about, O(size · log k). Asked of the
root of a million nodes many times a second, that is the cost; a caller
who needs it that often should ask about smaller subtrees, or maintain
the ranking it needs alongside.
It is not a time series. A value is the current measurement and replaces
the previous one. To attribute a rate, turn each node's cumulative counter
into one first with Counter from github.com/org-runink/runi/rate; to
smooth it, Decayed or EWMA from github.com/org-runink/runi/drift; and to
ask whether a subtree's sum has changed regime, feed Sum to a detector
there.
Diff compares structure, not values, and sees states, not history: a
node removed and added back between two snapshots is invisible to it.

Changes
type Changes[K cmp.Ordered] struct

Changes is what Diff found, each list in increasing key order.
To turn the tree a was taken from into the structure of b, in an order
that never needs a node that is not there yet and never forms a cycle:

AddRoot every Added node.
Move every Moved node to a root: Move(m.ID, m.ID).
Move every Added and every Moved node to its parent in b. Each such
edge is an edge of b, and every node it could pass through is now
linked by edges of b too, so none of these moves can be refused.
Remove the Removed nodes: by now their children are Removed nodes
too, so RemoveSubtree on each one still present (or Remove, deepest
first) finishes the job.

Defined in tree/snapshot.go.

Metric
type Metric int

Metric chooses the value TopK ranks nodes by.
Defined in tree/topk.go.
Move
type Move[K cmp.Ordered] struct

Move is a node whose parent changed between two snapshots. A root's parent
is written as the node itself, as Tree.Move accepts it, so From == ID means
the node was a root and To == ID that it became one.
Defined in tree/snapshot.go.
Snapshot
type Snapshot[K cmp.Ordered] struct

Snapshot is an immutable copy of a tree's structure: which nodes there
were and the parent of each, a root recorded as its own parent. It holds
no values. Keep one, and Diff it against a later one to see what changed.
It is stored as a key-sorted list of (node, parent) pairs, so Diff is a
single merge of two sorted lists. The zero value is an empty snapshot.
Safe to copy and to share between goroutines.
Defined in tree/snapshot.go.
Tree
type Tree[K cmp.Ordered] struct

Tree is a forest of nodes keyed by K, each carrying a float64 value of its
own, with the subtree sum and the subtree maximum of every node kept up to
date as single nodes change.
Every query is deterministic: children are kept in key order, and every tie
(two equal maxima, two equal top-k values) goes to the smaller key. That is
why K is cmp.Ordered rather than comparable.
A root is its own parent. That is the usual parent-array representation of
a forest (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms,
3rd ed., §21.3, "the root of each tree is its own parent"), and the package
uses it everywhere a parent is named: Parent of a root returns the root,
Add(id, id) adds a root, Move(id, id) makes id a root, and a Snapshot or a
Move records a root's parent as the node itself. A loop that walks up by
Parent stops when the parent equals the node; Path does that walk for you.
Subtree sums use compensated summation (see Set), and subtree maxima a
max-heap of children per node (see Max). Structure changes cost the depth
of the node times log of the branching, plus a shift of the sibling list;
the doc of each method says which. Indices, not pointers, link the nodes,
and removed slots are reused, so a long-lived tree that adds and removes
nodes at a steady rate does not grow.
The zero value is an empty tree, ready to use; New returns the same. A
Tree must not be copied after first use (a copy shares its storage), and is
not safe for concurrent use.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Diff
func Diff[K cmp.Ordered](a, b Snapshot[K]) Changes[K]

Diff compares two snapshots: nodes only in b are Added, nodes only in a
Removed, and nodes in both whose parent differs Moved — never Removed and
Added, so a node that changed place keeps its identity. O(len(a)+len(b)),
a single merge of the two sorted lists; the result is deterministic.
Snapshots see states, not history: a node removed and added again under
a different parent between a and b shows as Moved, and one removed and
added again under the same parent does not show at all.
Defined in tree/snapshot.go.
ErrInvalid
var ErrInvalid = errors.New("tree: invalid argument")

ErrInvalid is wrapped by every error this package returns: an argument the
tree cannot accept in its current state. The more specific sentinels below
wrap it too, so errors.Is(err, ErrInvalid) holds for all of them. Match
with errors.Is; the message text is not part of the API.

Len is the number of nodes in the snapshot.

Parent is id's parent when the snapshot was taken, id itself for a root;
ok is false when id was not in the tree. O(log n).
Defined in tree/snapshot.go.
Tree.Add
func (t *Tree[K]) Add(id, parent K) error

Add adds id as a new leaf under parent, or as a root when parent == id.
It fails with ErrExists if id is already in the tree, ErrUnknown if parent
is not, and ErrInvalid if id is a NaN. A new node's own value is 0, so the
sums do not change; the maxima can (a 0 can beat negative values, or tie a
0 and win on key).
Cost: O(b) to insert into the parent's key-ordered child list, b the
number of siblings, plus O(depth · log b) to update the maxima above it.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.AddRoot

AddRoot adds id as a new root. It fails with ErrExists if id is already in
the tree, and with ErrInvalid if id is a NaN (which no map lookup could
ever find again). A new node's own value is 0.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Children
func (t *Tree[K]) Children(id K, dst []K) []K

Children appends id's children to dst in increasing key order and returns
the extended slice. It appends nothing when id is a leaf or not in the
tree. O(b); it does not allocate when dst has room for the children.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Depth
func (t *Tree[K]) Depth(id K) (depth int, ok bool)

Depth is the number of edges from id up to its root: 0 for a root. ok is
false when id is not in the tree. O(depth): depths are not stored, because
keeping them would make Move cost the size of the subtree moved.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Len
func (t *Tree[K]) Len() int

Len is the number of nodes.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Max
func (t *Tree[K]) Max(id K) (v float64, at K, ok bool)

Max is the largest own value in id's subtree, id included, and the node
that holds it; on a tie, the smaller key. ok is false, and v NaN, when id
is not in the tree. O(1).
Each node keeps its subtree maximum, and its children in a binary max-heap
ordered by their subtree maxima (J. W. J. Williams, "Algorithm 232:
Heapsort", Commun. ACM 7(6), 1964; Cormen et al., Introduction to
Algorithms, ch. 6), so a node's maximum is the larger of its own value and
the top of its heap. Rescanning the children instead would be simpler, and
costs O(b) whenever the maximum decreases — under a parent with a hundred
thousand children, every update to the busiest one. With the heap a change
costs O(log b) at each level and stops at the first level where the maximum
does not change. The heap lives in the node, takes one slot per child, and
is rearranged in place, so updates do not allocate.
Defined in tree/values.go.
Tree.Move
func (t *Tree[K]) Move(id, newParent K) error

Move makes newParent the parent of id, carrying id's whole subtree with
it; Move(id, id) makes id a root. Moving a node to the parent it already
has does nothing.
A move under id itself or under any of its descendants would cut the
subtree off from every root into a cycle, and fails with ErrCycle. The
check walks up from newParent towards its root looking for id: O(depth of
newParent), no extra memory, and nothing else in the tree is touched.
Unknown id or newParent fails with ErrUnknown.
Cost: the check, plus for each of the old and new parent O(b) to update
its child list and O(depth · log b) to update sums and maxima on the path
to the root. The subtree's own sums and maxima are unchanged, so its size
does not matter.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Own
func (t *Tree[K]) Own(id K) float64

Own is id's own value, 0 if never set, NaN if id is not in the tree. O(1).
Defined in tree/values.go.
Tree.Parent
func (t *Tree[K]) Parent(id K) (parent K, ok bool)

Parent returns id's parent, or id itself when id is a root. ok is false
only when id is not in the tree. O(1).
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Path
func (t *Tree[K]) Path(id K, dst []K) []K

Path appends the keys from id's root down to id, both included, to dst and
returns the extended slice. It appends nothing when id is not in the tree.
O(depth); it does not allocate when dst has room for depth+1 keys.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Rebuild
func (t *Tree[K]) Rebuild()

Rebuild recomputes every subtree sum from the own values, bottom-up, each
as a fresh compensated sum, discarding whatever error the incremental
updates accumulated. O(n); it allocates a list of the nodes in order. It
is never needed for correctness; see Set for when it helps precision.
Maxima are exact comparisons, never drift, and are left as they are.
Defined in tree/values.go.
Tree.Remove
func (t *Tree[K]) Remove(id K) error

Remove removes id, which must be a leaf; a node with children fails with
ErrHasChildren, an unknown one with ErrUnknown. Its own value leaves the
sums of its ancestors.
Only leaves, because the point of the tree is attribution: removing an
inner node would either drop its descendants' values from every ancestor's
sum without the caller having said so, or silently hand them to the
grandparent. Remove bottom-up, move the children elsewhere first, or say
explicitly that the whole subtree goes with RemoveSubtree.
Cost: O(b + depth · log b), as Add.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.RemoveSubtree
func (t *Tree[K]) RemoveSubtree(id K) (removed int, err error)

RemoveSubtree removes id and all its descendants, and returns how many
nodes that was. Their values leave the sums of id's ancestors. Unknown id
fails with ErrUnknown and removes nothing.
Cost: O(subtree size) plus, for id's parent, the cost of Remove. It
allocates a list of the subtree's slots.
Defined in tree/tree.go.
Tree.Set
func (t *Tree[K]) Set(id K, v float64) error

Set sets id's own value to v and updates the subtree sum and maximum of
every ancestor. It does not allocate.
Sums are updated incrementally, not recomputed: v is added to, and the old
value subtracted from, the sum of id and of each ancestor, O(depth). Done
naively that loses precision for good: after a node goes from 0 to 1e16
and back, a sibling's 1 has been rounded away from every ancestor's sum
(1e16 + 1 is 1e16 in float64) and nothing ever brings it back. So each sum
is kept as a pair, a running sum and a running compensation that collects
exactly the low-order part each addition rounded off, which is Neumaier's
improvement of Kahan's compensated summation (A. Neumaier, "Rundungsfehler-
analyse einiger Verfahren zur Summation endlicher Summen", ZAMM 54, 1974;
see N. J. Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed.,
SIAM 2002, §4.3). Sum returns sum + compensation.
The error of a compensated sum of n terms x₁…xₙ with exact total S is at
most u·|S| + γ²·Σ|xᵢ|, u = 2⁻⁵³ and γ = n·u/(1−n·u) (T. Ogita, S. M. Rump
and S. Oishi, "Accurate sum and dot product", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26(6),
2005, Proposition 4.5, for the equivalent Sum2). Every Set below a node
adds two terms to that node's sum. The first part is the rounding of the
answer itself, the best any method can do. The second is the drift, and
it grows with the cube of the number of updates below the node (the
square from γ², once more from Σ|xᵢ|): for values about as large as the
sum it is some tens of u·|S|, a relative 1e-14, after 10⁶ updates, and
1e-11 after 10⁷. That is a guarantee for the worst case, not the typical
error. The test that holds the bound (10⁶ updates, values over fifteen
orders of magnitude, random signs, up to 36 levels deep) also requires
that no node's error exceeds u·|S|, which holds; a naive running sum on
the same updates is off by 0.1 at the root and by more than 10¹⁵·u·|S| at
a node whose sum nearly cancels. Rebuild recomputes every sum from the own
values and drops the drift; a tree that must guarantee eleven digits
through more than 10⁷ updates per node should call it that often.
v must be finite and |v| ≤ 2⁹⁶⁰ (about 1e289), or Set fails with ErrInvalid
and changes nothing. Unlike the streaming summaries elsewhere in this
module, which skip a non-finite reading and carry on, a value here is
state that every ancestor's sum shares: a NaN, once added, makes every sum
above it NaN, and no later Set can subtract it out again (NaN − NaN is
NaN); an infinity does the same through ∞ − ∞. Skipping silently would
leave the previous value attributed as if it were current. Rejecting lets
the caller decide what a missing reading means: often 0, sometimes the
last good value. The bound keeps every sum, and every intermediate term,
finite. Unknown id fails with ErrUnknown.
The maximum is updated by walking up the same path, repairing each
ancestor's heap of children (see Max): O(depth · log b) for branching b,
and it stops as soon as an ancestor's maximum is unchanged, which for most
updates is immediately.

TopK appends to dst the k nodes of id's subtree with the largest value by
metric, largest first, ties to the smaller key, and returns the extended
slice. id itself is not a candidate: the question is which descendants
account for most of id, and by BySum id would always come first with a
value the caller already has from Sum. Fewer than k are appended when id
has fewer descendants. It appends nothing when id is not in the tree, k ≤ 0,
or metric is neither ByOwn nor BySum.
Candidates come from every depth, so by BySum a node and its own parent
can both appear: a child that accounts for most of its parent ranks just
below it. That is the honest answer to "which subtrees are heaviest"; to
rank only id's direct children, use Children and Sum.
It walks the whole subtree, O(size · log k), keeping the best k so far in
a bounded min-heap held in dst's own storage beyond its current length,
then sorts that in place (heapsort). It does not allocate when dst has
room for k more entries.

runi/sustain
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/sustain"

Package sustain keeps a decision made on a noisy series from flapping
around its threshold.
A check of the form "x > limit" run on every reading of a live series
changes its answer every time noise carries x across the limit, and
whatever the answer drives — an alert, a throttle, a scale-up — changes
with it. The remedies are old and well understood: two levels instead of
one, a condition that must persist before it counts, a majority over the
last few readings, a bound on how fast an output may move. This package
provides each as a small value type that takes one reading at a time,
with the time the reading was taken.
Which to use:

Hysteresis is an on/off state with a set level and a separate clear
level (a Schmitt trigger), High or Low, and an optional minimum dwell
in a state after each change. The deadband between the levels absorbs
noise smaller than itself.
Debounce follows a boolean condition only after it has held for a time
and/or a number of consecutive readings, with separate delays for on
and off: the on-delay and off-delay of alarm management.
NofM is on while at least Need of the last Size readings (Size ≤ 64)
are past a level: it escalates on a condition that holds most of the
time, which a Debounce would keep restarting.
Band classifies a reading into ordered levels — below, inside, above;
normal, warning, critical — with a deadband on every edge.
Slew bounds how fast an output follows its input, in units per second
of the readings' own time, with separate rates up and down.

They compose. Debounce takes any condition, so a Hysteresis's state or a
Band's level compared with a constant can feed it; a Slew in front of any
of them smooths what they see, and one behind a controller smooths what it
does.
h,  := sustain.NewHysteresis(sustain.High, 90, 80, time.Minute)
d,  := sustain.NewDebounce(sustain.Delay{For: 30 * time.Second}, sustain.Delay{})
for r := range readings {
    if d.Update(h.Update(r.Value, r.At), r.At) {
        log.Printf("hot for %v", d.InState(r.At))
    }
}
Time comes only from the at argument of each Update; nothing here reads
the clock or sleeps, so every type is as testable as the caller's clock
is. Times are compared with time.Time.After and differenced with
time.Time.Sub, which use the monotonic reading time.Now attaches, so a
wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort an interval.
Two rules hold for every type, and tests hold each type to them:

A reading whose time is not after the last accepted reading — a
duplicate, a clock stepped back, readings delivered out of order — is
skipped. There is no right place to put a late reading in a state
machine that has already acted on later ones, and a duplicate would
count twice toward a number of readings.
A NaN or ±Inf reading is skipped. A missed reading should not decide a
state, and "no reading" is not evidence for either side of a level.

A skipped reading is counted in Skipped and leaves no other trace: the
state, the time of the last reading and any run or window are exactly as
if it had never been offered. A series that is mostly skipped readings is
visible as one.
Every Update does O(1) work in fixed memory — Band's is O(levels crossed)
— and allocates nothing; a test holds each to zero. Every type is safe to
copy and none is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or
guard it. Constructor errors wrap ErrInvalid.
What this package does not do
It does not choose levels, deadbands or delays. Those depend on the
series' noise and on what a late or a false decision costs, which only the
caller knows. ISA-18.2 and its technical report on alarm design tabulate
starting deadbands and delays by measurement type for process plant
signals; a deadband a few times the noise's standard deviation, measured
over a stretch known to be normal (Welford in
github.com/org-runink/runi/drift), is the usual first try elsewhere.
It does not detect change. A deadband stops flapping around a level you
chose; whether the series' level has itself moved is a question for the
detectors in github.com/org-runink/runi/drift, whose output can then drive
a Debounce here.
It sees only readings. A Debounce's "held for 30 s" is "every reading for
30 s agreed"; a gap between readings is not seen, so a run of two readings
a minute apart has lasted a minute. A caller who needs to treat a long gap
as breaking a run should check it (Intervals in
github.com/org-runink/runi/rate watches gaps) and call Reset.
It does not reorder or interpolate. A late reading is dropped, not placed;
a Slew's output exists only at readings, and nothing between them is
computed.
It never acts. Nothing here alerts, throttles or retries; each type
returns a state or a number, and what follows from it is the caller's.

Band
type Band struct

Band classifies each reading into one of an ordered set of levels — below,
inside and above a band; normal, warning and critical — with hysteresis at
every boundary.
The levels are numbered 0 to len(edges), lowest values first, and edge k
separates level k from level k+1. Each edge is a Schmitt trigger with its
own pair of levels, so a reading that sits near a boundary does not flip
between the levels on either side of it: noise whose peak-to-peak amplitude
is less than an edge's Up − Down cannot carry the level across that edge
both ways. A reading may move the level several steps at once; a reading
strictly between an edge's Down and Up leaves that edge where it was.
For a band where the middle is normal, give two edges: level 0 is below,
1 inside, 2 above. For severities that rise with the value, level 0 is
normal and each edge is a more severe alarm; for severities that rise as
the value falls, number them from the top (severity = len(edges) − level).
The edges must be in order: both Up and Down strictly increasing from one
edge to the next. Then the level is always the number of edges whose
trigger is on, as if each edge were a separate Hysteresis, and the tests
hold Band to exactly that.
Dwell is an optional minimum time at a level after a change, as for
Hysteresis: a reading less than dwell after the last change cannot move the
level, is counted in Held, and is not remembered. It applies only after a
change; the first move from level 0 is never delayed. With a dwell, the
level is no longer the count of separate triggers, since one change holds
back every edge.
The level starts at 0. NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are
readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading; both are
counted in Skipped and leave no other trace.
Method: the multi-level alarm with a deadband on each setpoint of
ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries;
each edge is the trigger of O. H. Schmitt, "A thermionic trigger", Journal
of Scientific Instruments 15(1), 1938.
NewBand copies the edges; Update never changes them, so a copy of a Band
shares them safely and is independent of the original. The zero value
has no edges and is always at level 0; build one with NewBand. Not safe for
concurrent use.
Defined in sustain/band.go.
Debounce
type Debounce struct

Debounce is an on/off state that follows a boolean condition only once the
condition has held, continuously, for a set time or number of readings.
The condition is anything the caller decides per reading: a value over a
level, a check that failed, the output of a Hysteresis. A condition that
flickers — true for one reading in a run of false ones — is noise, and
Debounce ignores it: the state turns on only after the condition has been
true on every reading of a run that satisfies the on Delay, and turns off
only after it has been false on every reading of a run that satisfies the
off Delay. A single reading that agrees with the current state ends the run
and the count starts again. The two delays are separate because the costs
are: a late alarm and a late all-clear are different mistakes.
"Continuously" means as far as the readings show. The time a run has lasted
is the time between its first reading and the current one; what happened
between two readings is not seen, so a run of two readings an hour apart
has lasted an hour.
Readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading (duplicates, a
clock stepped back, readings delivered out of order) are skipped and
counted in Skipped; they neither extend nor break a run.
Method: the on-delay and off-delay timers of ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management
of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries, where an alarm is annunciated
only after its condition has persisted for the on-delay and returns to
normal only after the return has persisted for the off-delay. The count of
consecutive readings is the sampled form of the same rule, the integrating
debouncer of switch-input practice.
The zero value is a Debounce with no delays, ready to use: it follows its
condition at every reading. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.
Defined in sustain/debounce.go.

one, and over at least Readings consecutive readings. Both must be met when
both are set. The zero Delay is no delay: the state follows at the first
reading. Readings of 0 and 1 are the same requirement.

Hysteresis
type Hysteresis struct

Hysteresis is an on/off state with separate levels for turning on and
turning off: a Schmitt trigger.
A single threshold under noise flaps: a reading that sits near it crosses
it on every other sample, and every crossing is a change of state. Two
levels stop that. For a High alarm the state turns on at a reading at or
above set, and turns off only at a reading at or below clear, with
clear 
Dwell is an optional minimum time in a state after a change, the minimum
on-time and off-time of relay and thermostat practice. A reading less than
dwell after the last change cannot change the state again; it is counted
in Held. It is not remembered either: once the dwell has passed, the state
changes at the first reading that is itself past the opposite level. The
dwell guards against a fast series that is truly crossing both levels
(a deadband narrower than the swings), which no deadband alone can stop.
It applies only after a change: the first change, from the initial off
state, is never delayed.
The state starts off. The first reading is judged like any other, so a
series that starts at or past set turns the state on at once.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are readings whose time is not
after the last accepted reading (duplicates, a clock stepped back, readings
delivered out of order); both are counted in Skipped and leave no other
trace.
Method: O. H. Schmitt, "A thermionic trigger", Journal of Scientific
Instruments 15(1), 1938. The deadband as an alarm setting:
ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process
Industries, where it is the distance a signal must move back past the
setpoint before the alarm returns to normal (clear = set − deadband for a
high alarm).
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewHysteresis. Safe to copy,
not safe for concurrent use.
Defined in sustain/hysteresis.go.
NofM
type NofM struct

NofM is on while at least Need of the last Size readings are past a level:
the N of M of its name.
It sits between a plain threshold, which fires on one reading, and a
Debounce, which needs every reading of a run: a condition that holds most
of the time but not always — three readings over in five, with one dip
back under between them — escalates here and would keep restarting a
Debounce. For a High level a reading is past it when it is at or above it;
for Low, at or below.
The last Size outcomes are kept as bits of one word, newest in the lowest
bit, so an update is a shift, a mask and a population count: no buffer and
no allocation, and the count is exact. Before Size readings have been
accepted the window holds those there are, and Need of them suffice. NofM
has no deadband of its own; the window is its smoothing.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped and take no slot, so "the last Size"
means the last Size finite readings. Readings whose time is not after the last
accepted reading are skipped too. Both are counted in Skipped.
Method: the M-of-N rule is the "binary integration" (double-threshold)
detector of radar, M. I. Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems,
McGraw-Hill; the same rule over a
control chart's zones gives the run rules of the Western Electric
Statistical Quality Control Handbook, 1956 ("two out of three beyond two
sigma", "four out of five beyond one sigma"), as tabulated in D. C.
Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical Quality Control, Wiley.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewNofM. Safe to copy, not
safe for concurrent use.
Defined in sustain/nofm.go.
Slew
type Slew struct

Slew is a rate limiter: its output moves toward its input, but by no more
than a set amount per second of the readings' own time.
A setpoint or a control output that jumps — a limit cut in half in one
step, a replica count that doubles — can do more harm by the jump than by
the new value. Slew passes the input through, but bounds how fast the
output may follow: over an interval of Δt seconds between readings it rises
by at most rise·Δt and falls by at most fall·Δt, and it never passes the
input. A step in the input becomes a ramp; an input that stays within reach
is followed exactly. Separate rates for rising and falling allow the usual
asymmetric forms, such as fast to back off and slow to return; either may be
+Inf, which removes the limit in that direction.
The bound is on the readings' timestamps, not on the number of readings:
readings close together move the output a little each, readings far apart
a lot. The first reading sets the output to the input, since there is no
earlier output to limit. The arithmetic is the bound itself: when limited,
the output is exactly old ± rate·Δt as one floating-point addition rounds
it, so it never moves farther than that rounded sum. A step smaller than
the spacing of floating-point numbers at the output's magnitude rounds to
no movement at all.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are readings whose time is not
after the last accepted reading; both are counted in Skipped and leave no
other trace. The next accepted reading's Δt then covers the skipped
interval, so the output may make up the movement it was allowed then.
Method: the rate limiter of control engineering, the nonlinear element that
bounds the derivative of a signal, treated among the actuator limitations
that cause integrator windup in K. J. Åström and T. Hägglund, Advanced PID
Control, ISA, 2006; here in sampled form, with the bound taken over each
irregular interval.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewSlew. Safe to copy, not
safe for concurrent use.

runi/throttle
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/throttle"

Package throttle caps how often something may act: per interval, per
target, and after failures.
Anything that acts on its own — restarts a process, scales a pool, drains
a node, retries a request — can act too often when what it watches
misbehaves, and its actions can then do more harm than the fault. The
remedies are old and well understood: a rate with a burst allowance, a
fixed allowance per window, a minimum interval per target, a growing
random delay between retries, and a switch that stops trying something
that keeps failing. This package provides each as a small type that is
told the time of every call.
Which to use:

Bucket is a token bucket: on average rate actions per second, at most
burst at once. Over any stretch of time t it allows at most
burst + ⌊rate·t⌋. Kept in integer nanoseconds as the generic cell rate
algorithm's theoretical arrival time, so it does not drift.
Quota is at most N actions in each window of length W, windows laid
from an origin the caller chooses: "5 per hour, on the hour". It says
how many remain and when the window ends.
Cooldown lets each key act at most once per period, for any comparable
key; keys are forgotten once their period ends, in O(1) amortised
time, and an optional cap bounds how many are tracked.
Backoff draws the delays between retries: exponential, capped, and
randomised by full or decorrelated jitter from a source the caller
seeds.
Breaker is a circuit breaker: closed, open and half-open, opening after
consecutive failures and probing before it closes again.

They compose: each answers "may I act now?", and an action that must pass
several caps asks each of them.
limit,  := throttle.NewBucket(0.1, 3)  // one restart per 10 s, 3 at once
each,  := throttle.NewCooldownstring
for ev := range unhealthy {
    if each.Allow(ev.Service, ev.At) && limit.Allow(ev.At) {
        restart(ev.Service)
    }
}
The order matters when an action is refused: a cap asked first spends its
allowance even when a later one refuses. Ask the scarcest last, or use
the query methods (Tokens, Remaining, Next) first.
Time comes only from the at argument of each call; nothing here reads the
clock or sleeps, so every type is as testable as the caller's clock is.
Backoff takes no time at all: it returns a delay, and waiting is the
caller's. Times are compared and differenced with time.Time's own
methods, which use the monotonic reading time.Now attaches, so a
wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort an interval.
One rule holds for every timed type, and tests hold each type to it: a
time before the latest one the type has seen is taken as the latest, and
counted in Late. Time never runs backwards, so a clock stepped back, or
calls delivered out of order, cannot refill a bucket, reopen a window,
end a cooldown or end an open period early; at worst they make the type
wait until the clock passes where it was. A call at the latest time is
not late. Query methods (Tokens, Next, Remaining, WindowEnd) apply the
same rule and change nothing.
Allow and AllowN on Bucket and Quota, Breaker's Allow and Record and
Backoff's Next do O(1) work and allocate nothing; so does Cooldown's
Allow, in O(1) amortised, on a key it already tracks or once its table
has reached its working size. A test holds each to zero. Bucket, Quota and
Breaker are plain values, safe to copy. A Cooldown holds a table and a
Backoff a random source by reference, and a copy shares them. None is
safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or guard it.
Constructor errors wrap ErrInvalid.
What this package does not do
It does not choose rates, windows, periods or thresholds, and has no
defaults. They follow from how much harm one action can do and how fast
the thing acted on recovers, which only the caller knows. The literature
cited on each type describes mechanisms, not settings.
It does not wait. Next, NextN and Backoff.Next say when or how long;
sleeping, timers and contexts are the caller's.
It does not coordinate. Every cap is local to the value that holds it;
several processes each with a Bucket of rate r together allow up to
r times as many. A limit shared across processes needs shared state —
one owner the others ask — which this package does not provide.
It does not adapt. Rates and thresholds are fixed at construction; it
does not raise a rate while actions succeed or lower it when they fail,
as the additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease rule of V. Jacobson,
"Congestion Avoidance and Control", ACM SIGCOMM 1988, does for a
transport's window.
It does not judge results. What counts as a failure for a Breaker, and
whether an error is worth a retry, is the caller's decision.
It does not keep a log of actions. Quota counts per fixed window and
Bucket refills continuously; a sliding window over a log of every action
is exact over every stretch but costs memory per action, and is not here.
It does not persist. A process that restarts starts every cap afresh,
with full buckets and closed breakers.

Backoff
type Backoff struct

Backoff draws the delays to wait between retries of a failed action:
growing, capped, and random, so that many callers that failed together do
not retry together.
Plain exponential backoff, base·2ⁿ before the n-th retry, spreads one
caller's retries out but keeps callers that failed at the same moment in
step: they retry at the same moments and collide again. Randomising each
delay breaks the lockstep. Of the schemes compared in M. Brooker,
"Exponential Backoff And Jitter", AWS Architecture Blog, 2015, this
provides the two the article recommends:

FullJitter: uniform on [0, min(cap, base·2ⁿ)]. The delays grow as plain
backoff does, but each is anywhere from zero to that ceiling; in the
article's simulation it needed the least total work.
DecorrelatedJitter: min(cap, uniform[base, 3·prev]), starting from
prev = base. Each delay depends on the last instead of on the attempt
number, grows by up to three times per retry, and never falls below
base.

Exponential backoff itself is that of R. M. Metcalfe and D. R. Boggs,
"Ethernet: Distributed Packet Switching for Local Computer Networks",
Communications of the ACM 19(7), 1976, where a station that collides
waits a random number of slots drawn from a range that doubles with each
collision; IEEE 802.3 stops doubling after 10 collisions and gives up
after 16. This package stops at cap and never gives up: how many retries
to make is the caller's decision.
Randomness comes only from the source given to NewBackoff — a
*rand.Rand, or a rand.PCG or rand.ChaCha8 from math/rand/v2, seeded by the
caller — so a Backoff with a seeded source draws the same delays on every
run. Integers in a range are drawn without bias by the multiply-and-reject
method of D. Lemire, "Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval", ACM
Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 29(1), 2019. Delays are
whole nanoseconds; every value of the range, both ends included, is
equally likely before the cap is applied.
Backoff computes delays and does nothing else: it does not sleep, and it
takes no time because no delay depends on one. The caller waits, retries,
and calls Reset after a success.
The zero value is not usable (Next panics on it); build one with
NewBackoff. A copy shares the source with the original, and so draws from
the same stream. Not safe for concurrent use, and neither are the sources
math/rand/v2 provides.
Defined in throttle/backoff.go.
Breaker
type Breaker struct

Breaker stops calling something that keeps failing, and tries it again,
carefully, after a while.
It has three states:

Closed: Allow admits every call. Record counts consecutive failures; a
success resets the count, and threshold failures in a row open the
breaker.
Open: Allow refuses every call until openFor has passed since the
breaker opened; then the breaker is half-open.
HalfOpen: Allow admits up to probes calls, and refuses the rest. If any
probe fails, the breaker opens again for another openFor; once probes
of them have succeeded, it closes.

Every change of state is counted in Transitions, and Since is the time of
the latest. The move from Open to HalfOpen happens at the first Allow,
Record or State call at or after the end of the open period, and Since is
that call's time.
Results are matched to calls only by count. In HalfOpen a Record counts as
a probe's result only while an admitted probe has not yet reported; any
other result — from a call admitted while the breaker was still closed,
arriving late — is ignored, as is every Record while the breaker is Open.
A probe whose result is never recorded holds its place, and once every
probe is held the breaker stays half-open; record a timed-out probe as a
failure.
Method: the Circuit Breaker pattern of M. T. Nygard, Release It! Design
and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed., Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018,
chapter 5 (stability patterns): closed, open and half-open, a failure
threshold to open, a timeout to try again, and a trial call to decide.
Allowing more than one trial (probes > 1) and requiring all of them to
succeed is a stricter form of the same rule.
A time before the latest one the breaker has seen is taken as the latest
(and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot end an open period
early.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewBreaker. Safe to copy,
not safe for concurrent use.
Defined in throttle/breaker.go.
Bucket
type Bucket struct

Bucket is a token bucket: it allows on average rate actions per second,
and up to burst of them at once after a quiet spell.
The bucket holds at most burst tokens and gains one every 1/rate seconds;
an action takes one token, or n for AllowN, and is refused when there are
not enough. Over any stretch of time of length t, then, at most
burst + ⌊t·rate⌋ tokens are taken: the bucket's whole content at the start
plus what it earned during the stretch. A test holds every Bucket to that
bound over every pair of its own allowed actions.
Method: the generic cell rate algorithm (GCRA) in its virtual-scheduling
form, ATM Forum, Traffic Management Specification Version 4.0
(af-tm-0056.000), 1996, and ITU-T Recommendation I.371, Traffic control
and congestion control in B-ISDN. Rather than a count of tokens that grows
with time, GCRA keeps a theoretical arrival time (TAT): the time at which
the bucket would be full again if nothing more were taken. A request for n
tokens at time t conforms when TAT + n·T − burst·T ≤ t, T being the
interval between tokens, and then moves TAT to max(TAT, t) + n·T. That is
the token bucket of A. S. Tanenbaum and D. J. Wetherall, Computer
Networks, 5th ed., Pearson, 2011, §5.4 (traffic shaping), counted in time
instead of tokens; the leaky bucket of J. S. Turner, "New directions in
communications (or which way to the information age?)", IEEE
Communications Magazine 24(10), 1986, is the same rule seen from the
other side.
Here TAT is kept as a debt: TAT minus the latest time, in whole
nanoseconds, between 0 and burst·T. T is 1/rate rounded once, in
NewBucket, to the nearest nanosecond (Interval reports it, Rate the rate it
gives); every step after that is integer addition, subtraction and
comparison, so a bucket run for years admits exactly what the arithmetic
says, with no rounding to accumulate and nothing to overflow.
A time before the latest one the bucket has seen is taken as the latest
(and counted in Late): a clock stepped back earns no tokens, and the
bucket resumes refilling only once the clock passes where it was.
The zero value refuses every action; build one with NewBucket. Safe to
copy, not safe for concurrent use.

Cooldown
type Cooldown[K comparable] struct

Cooldown lets each key act at most once per period: an action for a key is
allowed when the key has not been allowed one in the last period, and is
then the start of the key's next period. "Restart any one service at most
once every ten minutes."
The rule is exact. An action at t for a key last allowed at s is allowed
if and only if t − s ≥ period; a refused action does not move s. It is
the same rule as a Bucket of burst 1 and one token per period kept for
each key, and a test holds the two to the same decisions.
A key is forgotten once its period has passed, since from then on it would
be allowed anyway. Keys are kept in a queue in the order they were
allowed, which is also the order their periods end, because times never
run backwards here; so expired keys are always at the front. Every Allow
first drops the expired keys at the front, which costs O(1) amortised per
key ever allowed, and the table holds only keys allowed within the last
period. Sweep does the same dropping at a time of the caller's choosing,
for a table that may sit idle while holding many keys.
maxKeys, when positive, caps the keys tracked at once. When the table is
full of keys still within their period, an action for a new key is
refused and counted in Full: no tracked key is evicted to make room,
because an evicted key could then act again before its period ended, and
a cap on corrective actions should fail by acting less, not more. The
cap bounds memory: Go maps do not return memory on deletion, so the
table's footprint is its largest size, at most maxKeys entries.
Allow on a key already tracked does not allocate, nor does Allow on a key
whose period has ended once the table has reached its working size: the
slots expired keys leave are reused. Growing the table allocates.
A time before the latest one the cooldown has seen is taken as the
latest (and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot end a period
early.
The zero value is not usable (Allow panics on it: it has no table); build
one with NewCooldown, which returns a pointer. Not safe to copy (copies
share the table) and not safe for concurrent use.

Quota

Quota allows at most a fixed number of actions in each window of fixed
length: "no more than 5 restarts per hour, on the hour".
Windows are laid end to end from an origin the caller chooses: window k
is [origin + k·length, origin + (k+1)·length), for every integer k, so
windows before the origin exist too. A time on a boundary belongs to the
window it starts. The count starts again from zero at each boundary; a
window's unused actions do not carry over.
The guarantee is per window, not per stretch of time of the window's
length: actions taken at the end of one window and at the start of the
next fall in different windows, so a stretch of one window's length that
straddles a boundary can see up to twice the limit. Where that matters,
use a Bucket, whose bound holds over every stretch, or both.
Method: the jumping window of E. P. Rathgeb, "Modeling and performance
comparison of policing mechanisms for ATM networks", IEEE Journal on
Selected Areas in Communications 9(3), 1991, which also sets out the
boundary effect above. It suits quotas people read off a calendar or a
report — a count per hour, per day, per shift — that a token bucket's
continuous refill does not match.
A time before the latest one the quota has seen is taken as the latest
(and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot reopen an earlier
window. Window boundaries are computed from time.Time.Sub of the origin,
which saturates about 292 years away from it.

docs/develop/.title: Developer Guide
docs/develop/.body:
Developer Guide
How to build and test runi, the rules every change keeps, and how to add to it. The
source is at github.com/org-runink/runi, under
BSD-3-Clause.
Build and test
runi is one Go module with no dependencies, so a checkout and a supported Go toolchain
(1.24, 1.25 or 1.26) are all you need:
git clone https://github.com/org-runink/runi
cd runi
go vet ./...
go test -count=1 ./...
go test -race -count=1 ./...
gofmt -l .                              # must print nothing
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchtime 1x ./...   # every benchmark still compiles and runs

CI runs the same commands on each supported Go version, with GOTOOLCHAIN=local so a
newer toolchain is never fetched behind the test's back.
The rules a change keeps

Standard library only. go.mod has no require block, and CI fails if one appears,
if the module graph holds any other module, or if any imported package lives outside the
standard library.
Per-package coverage floors. Each package has its own coverage floor in CI. A change
that drops a package below its floor fails; a floor is raised when coverage genuinely
rises and never lowered.
Independent packages. A package imports no other runi package, so any one of them
can be taken alone or copied out. The one exception is barn, which stores its data in
avro's format and imports it.
Measured claims. A performance claim comes with the benchmark that produced it and
the hardware it ran on. The cross-language comparisons live in
benchmarks/.

Adding or changing a package

Put the package in its own top-level directory, with a package doc comment and runnable
Example functions that show the main use.
Bring its coverage to the level the other packages hold, and add its floor to the
coverage step of .github/workflows/ci.yml.
Regenerate the API Reference: the pages are generated from the source, and
the docs workflow fails if they are stale. Add the package to the docs workflow's list of
packages that must have an API page, and to Choosing a package.
Record the change in
CHANGELOG.md. Exported API
follows the compatibility rules.

Sign off every commit (git commit -s).
The documentation site
These pages are a Hugo site in website/ (the Hextra theme, vendored, so the build needs no
network):
hugo --source website --minify --destination ~/.cache/runi-docs-build

Security
Report a vulnerability privately, as described in
SECURITY.md, never in a public
issue.
